title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: In financial market infrastructure, distribution is borrowed from brokers, but liquidity is owned by the clearing house.
epigraph.author: Exchange Economics Principle

web_blocks.html: MCX runs an asset-light, B2B2C distribution model. Instead of signing up end-traders directly, it connects through registered Trading Members (TMs) and Clearing Members (CMs) [11][17]. These partners include discount retail brokers like Zerodha, Groww, and Angel One, bank-backed brokers, institutional desks, and prop algo firms [11][17]. Over 4 crore Unique Client Codes (UCCs) sit on the platform. Active traded F&O clients jumped ~90% YoY to 14.98 lakh in Q2 FY27, with 13.03 lakh in options and ~4 lakh in futures [11][12].

Institutional reach has also grown as SEBI opened non-farm commodity derivatives in phases. Over 250 Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs) have joined the exchange, alongside domestic mutual funds, Portfolio Management Services (PMS), and Category III Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs) [11][12]. For execution, MCX offers low-latency FIX/CTCL APIs and market data feeds on the TCS Commodity Derivatives Platform. However, its planned data-centre move and colocation rollout remains under SEBI review in 2026 [18].

MCX Clearing Corporation Limited (MCXCCL), a 100% subsidiary, anchors the clearing and delivery chain as central counterparty (CCP) to every trade [5][13]. MCXCCL runs daily mark-to-market settlement and collects upfront initial and extreme-loss margins. It also oversees SEBI-regulated vaults and approved warehouses for deliverable bullion and base metals. Its Core Settlement Guarantee Fund (SGF) stood at ₹1,367.29 crore in FY26 [5][13]. Clearing members park large cash and bank-guarantee collateral with MCXCCL. That cash float earns risk-free treasury interest—₹127 crore in FY26 and ₹52 crore in Q2 FY27—and creates deeply negative working capital (-465 days in FY26) [1][10].

web_blocks.takeaway: In FY26, MCX turned every ₹100 of sales into ₹71.33 of EBITDA, ₹57.86 of net profit, and ₹128.67 of Free Cash Flow. Clearing margin float boosted cash flow. Even without float inflows, core FCF converts at over 100% of PAT.

web_blocks.html: Post-TCS unit costs show why new volume drops fast to profit. In FY26, total IT costs were ₹104.74 crore, inside management's ₹90–110 crore target [13]. Employee costs were ₹180.11 crore, and benchmark license fees (paid to CME and other providers) were ₹107.96 crore [13]. Statutory and SGF charges stood at ₹164 crore [13]. Under SEBI's October 2024 True-to-Label rule, MCX replaced slab rebates with flat per-lakh fees (₹2.10 futures, ₹41.80 options premium) [14]. That flat fee structure simplified pricing math and ended broker-level fee arbitrage [14]. Debtor days also stayed tight at 10 days in FY26, down from 33 days in FY24 [1].

book_paragraphs: Think about how a normal manufacturing business grows: to double revenue, it has to buy twice as much steel, hire more factory shifts, and finance twice as much inventory. MCX works in the exact opposite way. Its distribution is handled by hundreds of brokers—from retail apps like Zerodha, Groww, and Angel One to institutional desks and 250-plus foreign portfolio investors—who bring 14.98 lakh active trading clients onto MCX's matching engine without MCX spending a rupee on consumer advertising.

Behind that order book sits MCX's clearing subsidiary, MCXCCL, backed by a ₹1,367 crore Settlement Guarantee Fund. Every broker and trader who wants to hold an open position has to park margin collateral with MCXCCL. That creates negative working capital—minus 465 days in FY26—meaning MCX gets paid upfront and holds cash collateral that earns steady treasury interest while trades clear.

Let's walk through the FY26 unit economics per ₹100 of revenue, because the numbers are astonishing. Out of every ₹100 MCX collected in FY26 (₹2,302 crore total), only ₹28.67 went to operating expenses—covering salaries, the ₹105 crore TCS technology bill, benchmark license fees, and statutory contributions. That left ₹71.33 in operating profit. After ₹3.39 for depreciation and adding ₹5.52 of treasury other income, MCX earned ₹73.41 before tax and ₹57.86 in pure net profit. And because clearing margin inflows swelled operating cash flow to ₹3,035 crore while capital expenditure was just ₹73 crore, Free Cash Flow hit ₹128.67 per ₹100 of revenue.

You and I should keep one nuance in mind, though: part of that ₹131.84 per ₹100 operating cash flow reflects rising clearing member margin deposits when market activity booms. If trading activity ever cools, some of that margin float flows back out. Even stripping out margin float entirely, MCX's underlying free cash flow still converts at roughly 100% of net profit—a hallmark of premier financial market infrastructure.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Separating Core FCF from Margin Float
book_callouts.text: When an exchange posts ₹3,035 crore of operating cash flow against ₹1,332 crore of net profit in FY26, do not mistake clearing-deposit inflows for permanent earnings. Core cash conversion is already ~100% of PAT because capex is tiny (₹73 crore); the extra ₹1,700 crore is working-capital float from member margins that expands in bull markets and contracts in quiet ones.

book_subsections.title: Borrowed Distribution, Owned Liquidity: The B2B2C Funnel
paragraphs: Most consumer-facing financial platforms spend heavily on marketing and customer acquisition to grow their user base. MCX avoids that entire cost layer through a B2B2C distribution model. The exchange connects to end-traders through hundreds of registered Trading Members and Clearing Members—ranging from high-velocity retail discount brokers like Zerodha, Groww, and Angel One to full-service bank-backed brokerages and proprietary algorithmic firms. More than 4 crore Unique Client Codes are registered on the exchange, and active traded F&O clients surged ~90% YoY to 14.98 lakh in Q2 FY27 (13.03 lakh in options and roughly 4 lakh in futures), all acquired by brokers rather than MCX's own balance sheet.

Institutional distribution has broadened alongside retail participation following SEBI's phased opening of non-agricultural commodity derivatives. Over 250 Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs) have now been onboarded onto the platform, joining domestic mutual funds, Portfolio Management Services (PMS), and Category III Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs). On the execution layer, MCX delivers low-latency FIX and CTCL APIs plus market data feeds over the TCS Commodity Derivatives Platform—though its planned third-party data-centre relocation and colocation rollout remains under SEBI regulatory review.

book_subsections.title: Inside MCXCCL: Margin Collateral, Vaults & Negative Working Capital
paragraphs: If brokers supply the distribution, MCX Clearing Corporation Limited (MCXCCL)—a 100% subsidiary—supplies the trust. Every trade executed on MCX is novated to MCXCCL, which acts as the central counterparty, runs daily mark-to-market settlement, and collects upfront initial and extreme-loss margins from clearing members. For deliverable bullion and base-metal contracts, MCXCCL also oversees SEBI-regulated vaulting, assaying, and accredited warehouses. Backing this clearing waterfall is a Core Settlement Guarantee Fund (SGF) of ₹1,367.29 crore as of FY26. Because clearing members must post cash and bank-guarantee collateral upfront before holding open positions, MCX operates with deeply negative working capital (-465 days in FY26) and earns risk-free treasury yields on cash margin float.

For you as a fundamental analyst, that clearing architecture explains why MCX's working-capital cycle looks upside-down compared to industrial companies: rather than tying up cash in receivables and inventory, MCX collects cash upfront—posting 10 debtor days in FY26 versus 33 days during the FY24 transition year—and earns treasury interest while holding collateral.

book_subsections.title: Dissecting Every ₹100 of FY26 Revenue
paragraphs: Walking line by line through MCX's audited FY26 unit economics per ₹100 of operating revenue shows why fixed-cost exchanges are among the most cash-generative businesses in finance. Out of ₹2,302 crore in FY26 operating revenue (₹100.00), total operating expenses consumed just ₹660 crore (₹28.67)—comprising ₹180.11 crore in employee costs, ₹104.74 crore in IT and technology expenses (comfortably inside management's ₹90–110 crore guidance), ₹107.96 crore in benchmark product license fees paid to providers like CME, and ₹164 crore in statutory and SGF-related items. That left ₹1,642 crore (₹71.33) in operating profit.

Below EBITDA, depreciation of ₹78 crore (₹3.39) from capitalizing the TCS platform was more than offset by ₹127 crore (₹5.52) of treasury and margin-float other income, yielding ₹1,690 crore (₹73.41) in profit before tax. After ₹358 crore (₹15.55, an effective ~21.2% tax rate), MCX delivered ₹1,332 crore (₹57.86) in pure net profit. On the cash flow statement, operating cash flow surged to ₹3,035 crore (₹131.84 per ₹100 of revenue), boosted by over ₹1,300 crore of clearing margin float inflows; with capital expenditure of just ₹73 crore (₹3.17), Free Cash Flow reached ₹2,962 crore (₹128.67). Strip out the cyclical margin-float swings, and underlying core FCF still converts at roughly 100% of net profit.
